scenes.name: the warp and S I M T
scenes.visual: Thirty-two individual thread lanes are grouped into a single unified block called a warp. A single instruction stream broadcasts to all 32 lanes simultaneously, each lane applying the instruction to its private register state.

beats.say: Thirty-two threads make a warp. Threads on a G P U never move one at a time; they always move in warps of thirty-two.
beats.show: Thirty-two individual blue thread lanes line up horizontally. A solid bracket binds them together under the label: 'one warp = 32 threads'.

beats.say: This model is called S I M T: single instruction, multiple threads.
beats.show: The label expands into 'SIMT: Single Instruction, Multiple Threads'. A single instruction card descends from the scheduler above.

beats.say: The instruction is fetched once, decoded once, and fired across all thirty-two lanes in lockstep.
beats.show: A single instruction packet splits into 32 simultaneous signals, illuminating all 32 lanes at the exact same instant.

beats.say: Every lane runs the exact same addition, but each lane points at its own data in its own registers.
beats.show: Under each lane, individual register slot indices show different values being added. Takeaway: 'the warp, not the thread, is the unit the hardware schedules'.

scenes.name: writing a kernel
scenes.visual: A two-line CUDA kernel code snippet. An animated index calculator maps block number and thread number to a global array offset, showing how adjacent threads naturally access adjacent memory addresses.

beats.say: A kernel is the program the G P U runs. It is written once, for a single thread, and launched across millions of threads.
beats.show: A clean code window displays two lines of C code: 'int i = blockIdx.x * 256 + threadIdx.x; c[i] = a[i] + b[i];'.

beats.say: Every thread runs those identical lines. The only thing that differs is its number.
beats.show: The hardware hands each thread its unique IDs: block number and thread number inside the block.

beats.say: Thread five of block three works out its index: three times two hundred and fifty-six plus five gives seven hundred and seventy-three.
beats.show: The formula evaluates step by step: 'i = 3 × 256 + 5 = 773'. An array pointer slides to element 773, at byte offset 3,092.

beats.say: Neighbouring threads get neighbouring indices. A warp of thirty-two threads reads thirty-two numbers lying side by side in memory: one hundred and twenty-eight consecutive bytes.
beats.show: A warp of threads from 64 to 95 highlights, pointing to 32 consecutive numbers in the array. A dimension bracket measures: '32 floats × 4 bytes = 128 contiguous bytes'. Takeaway: 'index arithmetic naturally organizes warps into contiguous memory requests'.

scenes.name: grids, blocks and cooperation
scenes.visual: The full launch hierarchy: a grid of 4,096 blocks, zooming into one block of 1,024 threads (32 warps). The block lands whole on one multiprocessor, where its threads share a private shared memory scratchpad.

beats.say: When software launches a kernel, it requests a grid of blocks.
beats.show: A massive 2D grid appears showing 4,096 blocks: 'Launch Grid · 1,048,576 total elements'.

beats.say: A block holds up to one thousand and twenty-four threads, which is thirty-two warps. The hardware places each block whole on one multiprocessor.
beats.show: One block expands to show its 32 warps (1,024 threads). It descends onto a multiprocessor tile, which keeps it until completion.

beats.say: A multiprocessor holds up to two thousand and forty-eight threads: two full blocks of one thousand and twenty-four, or eight blocks of two hundred and fifty-six.
beats.show: The multiprocessor tile shows two 1,024-thread blocks resident side by side, reaching the 2,048 thread ceiling.

beats.say: Shared memory belongs to a block. All its threads share the same scratchpad, which is why a block is the unit that cooperates.
beats.show: A shared memory scratchpad lights up inside the multiprocessor, accessible exclusively by threads within that block. Takeaway pill: 'blocks are the boundary of shared memory cooperation'.

scenes.name: lockstep and the cost of instruction decode
scenes.visual: A comparison between lockstep execution and independent instruction streams. A 128-bit binary instruction word (FFMA) is displayed. Scalar cores pay decode overhead on every operation; a warp decodes once for 32 operations.

beats.say: Thirty-two lanes moving in lockstep sounds rigid. Why not let every thread execute independently?
beats.show: A split view: Left shows 32 lanes moving in lockstep. Right shows 32 lanes jumping, branching, and fetching independently.

beats.say: Because independent execution requires thirty-two independent instruction decoders, branch trackers, and instruction caches.
beats.show: The right panel floods with complex decoder circuits, instruction buffers, and tracking logic, consuming enormous area.

beats.say: An instruction is itself a number, a hundred and twenty-eight bits of data stored in memory. Fetching and decoding it costs real energy and real silicon.
beats.show: A 128-bit binary instruction word displays: 'FFMA R140, R11, R4, R142'. Decoders split it into register fields and opcode logic.

beats.say: A scalar C P U core pays that decode cost for every single operation. A G P U warp pays it once and spreads it across thirty-two lanes.
beats.show: A cost comparison bar shows 32 decode operations for the scalar core versus 1 decode operation for the warp. Takeaway: 'sharing one instruction across 32 lanes frees the silicon that becomes arithmetic'.

checks.claim: Block 3 thread 5 global index: 3 * 256 + 5 = 773; byte offset at 4 bytes each = 3,092 bytes
32 consecutive float numbers * 4 bytes = 128 contiguous bytes
Array of 1,048,576 numbers with 256 threads per block requires 4,096 blocks
Multiprocessor capacity of 2,048 threads holds 2 blocks of 1,024 or 8 blocks of 256
